cards.title: A dashboard command that drives the app from any terminal
cards.notes:
One command, `dashboard`, that drives the app from any terminal, for the user and for Claude sessions outside the app's panes.

Today: `~/.local/bin/dashboard` only launches the app. The CLI (`project|pane|board`) is `node "$DASHBOARD_COMMAND"`, and only panes the app opened carry that variable, so a plain terminal or a Claude session elsewhere cannot use it.

Shape
- `dashboard` with no arguments opens the app, as today.
- `dashboard <noun> <verb> ...` runs the CLI: the same entry as `$DASHBOARD_COMMAND`, run with Electron's bundled Node (`ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1`), so no system node is needed. `rebuild.sh` installs the launcher in `~/.local/bin` (and the mac equivalent).
- `dashboard --help` and `dashboard <noun> --help` print usage written for a reader who has never seen the app; this is how Claude learns it.
- `$DASHBOARD_COMMAND` keeps working inside panes.

When it opens the app
- Commands that need the running app (`pane ...`, `project open/close/focus`) connect to its socket. If no app answers, they start it detached, wait for the socket (with a timeout and a clear failure line), then act.
- Commands that work on files never start the app: `board list/show/add/move/set/comment` read and write `.dashboard/board.json` through `board-store.ts`, and the app already watches the folder. Otherwise a Claude session in another repo running `dashboard board list` makes a window pop up.
- Starting the app from the command is the user's ask in the moment, so workflow-rule-1 is not broken; quitting, restarting or replacing it stays out of the command.

Commands (only what is used; add more when a real need shows up)
- project: list (open projects and those in ~/.dashboard/projects.yaml), open <name|aka|path>, close <name> (refused while a pane is busy, using closeRefusal), focus <name> (switch to its tab), init.
- pane: claim [--project], run <id> [--card|--worktree] "<prompt>", list [--all], send <id> "<text>" (type into a pane), release <id>.
- board: as today, plus --project <name> to name a board other than the current folder's.
- Not in scope: the drawer, notes, settings, layout. Mirroring the whole UI is weeks of work nobody calls.

Context outside a pane
- A pane knows its project; a plain terminal does not. `pane claim` outside a pane needs --project, else it is refused with a line saying so. `board` without --project uses the board of the current folder or its repo root, else refuses. Never guess a target.
- Refusals come back as values over the socket (errors-rule-2) and print through failureText (errors-rule-1); exit code non-zero.

Security
- The socket lets anything that reaches it start a Claude pane with any prompt in any project. Check it is created inside a user-only directory with mode 0600 (and fix it if not); the command must not widen access (no TCP, no world-readable path).

Teaching Claude
- A short section for the user's global CLAUDE.md, shipped in docs/command/README.md for the user to copy (the app does not edit the user's files): "`dashboard --help` drives the Dashboard app: open projects, dispatch panes, move cards."

Docs and tax
- docs/command: README, decisions (one name for launcher and CLI; app started only by commands that need it), history. Version bump (minor). Tests for the decisions: which commands need the app, the context resolution, the launch-and-wait timeout.

cards.title: Show what fills the context window from the Claude screen's context meter
cards.notes:
The Claude screen's status line shows 'context 14%' and used/size only. The Agent SDK's getContextUsage() answer (SDKControlGetContextUsageResponse) already carries the breakdown, and measureOf in src/shared/chat/chat-status.ts drops it: categories (tokens per row, with a stable id: system_prompt, system_tools, mcp_tools, custom_agents, memory_files, skills, messages, autocompact_buffer, free_space and the rest, plus kind used/free/buffer/deferred), memoryFiles (path, tokens), mcpTools (name, server, tokens). No extra call needed.

- A click on the context meter opens a small popup anchored to it: one row per category with tokens and percentage of the window, a thin coloured bar per row in the category's colour, then the memory files and the MCP tools, biggest first, each list capped with a 'N more' row. Deferred rows (not in the window) are shown apart or left out, decided on kind, never on the English name.
- Keyboard first (conventions-rule-1): a key opens the same popup (a row in src/shared/keys/actions.ts), and /context on the Claude screen does too, answered by the screen rather than sent to the session. Arrow keys walk the rows; Esc closes it and focus goes back to the prompt.
- The numbers are from the last measure (after each turn); the popup says when they were taken, and refreshes when a new measure lands while it is open.
- The breakdown shaping (sorting, capping, percentages, kind filter) is a small module with a test (workflow-rule-2). Help and docs/chat updated.

cards.title: Link dispatched worker panes from the Claude screen, and a workers popup in its status line
cards.notes:
When main dispatches with pane claim/run, the Claude screen shows only the tool's text ('started dashboard-terminal-2 in 2:1'). The user wants to jump to that pane, most of all from the manager tab, whose workers live on other projects' pages.

1. Links: every pane the screen mentions is a link. pane claim and pane run print a stable reference the renderer recognises (for example a dashboard://pane/<page>:<pane> url next to the human line), and the Claude screen's markdown renderer turns it into a link in tool output and in Claude's replies. Click or Enter on it switches to that pane's project page and focuses the pane. A pane already released shows as closed and does nothing but say so. Keyboard first: links are reachable from the transcript the way other links are.
2. Workers popup: a button on the status line, between 'ready' and the context meter, shows a count of this session's workers by state, e.g. '3 workers: 2 working, 1 done'. A click or a key (a row in src/shared/keys/actions.ts) opens a small popup anchored to it: one row per pane this session dispatched (on the manager, across every project), with project, pane, card or prompt's first words, and status from what pane list already knows (working, blocked waiting for permission, done, idle). Arrow keys walk the rows, Enter focuses the pane, Esc closes. Released panes drop off. The state updates live while it is open.
3. Which session dispatched a pane is recorded by main when pane run comes in over the socket; reuse what pane list and the session index already hold rather than a new store.

Related: card 0ee53751 (tell main when a worker finishes) uses the same pane state; build on each other's code, not two copies. The status decision (which states, how counted) and the link parsing are small modules with tests (workflow-rule-2). Help and docs/chat, docs/panes updated.

cards.title: Find a pane by what is in it
cards.notes:
Type `dev`, land in the pane running the dev server, whichever project it belongs to. The picker, but over panes rather than projects. Thirty panes across five projects is the size where a list stops working and a search starts.

fuzzy.ts and the picker overlay are already there, so the work is small. It depends on the naming card: without names there is nothing to match on but `terminal 3`.

Weigh it against the manager page first. If that page already lists every pane by name with Enter to jump, this is the same feature with a filter box on it, and the answer may be to put the filter there rather than build a second way in.

cards.title: Search every open project at once
cards.notes:
One box, ripgrep over every open project's folder, results grouped by project. Enter on a result opens that project's nvim at the line. Today `where did I write that` costs a guess about which project, a tab switch, and a search once you are there.

Spawning ripgrep is the easy half. The results list is the work: grouping, showing the matching line, and what to do about four hundred hits. It also needs ripgrep on the machine, or something slower behind it.

An overlay you open from anywhere, like the picker -- not a corner of the manager page. Searching is something you want from the pane you are in, not somewhere you navigate to first.

What it adds over `rg` in a pane, which already works and which your fingers know, is only the across-projects part. That is worth something with five open and nothing when you already know which one.

cards.title: A project remembers what its panes should be running
cards.notes:
Pane 1 runs the dev server, pane 2 the test watcher, pane 3 claude, stored with the project. The session card put the layout back and left this out on purpose -- same projects, same order, same view, same focused pane, and five empty shells. So every morning the same three commands go into the same three panes by hand.

Sending a command to a pane is plumbing that already exists. The new parts are where the commands are kept and when they fire: on launch, on opening the project, or only when asked.

The question that decides the design is what happens when something is already running. Reopen a project that is already open and `npm run dev` must not go into the pane that is running it -- you get a port already in use, or worse, two of them. Knowing whether a pane is busy is the same thing the send-to-many-panes card needs and does not have.

Only the last bit belongs to the manager page -- start all, stop all, one place to see what is up. The storing and running half stands on its own.

Decided: a command runs only into a fresh pane, never into one that already has something in it. Low for now, nothing runs locally today.

cards.title: Read a project's file in a view that does bidi
cards.notes:
Persian prose cannot be read in a pane and never will be, so the way to read a Persian roadmap or README is a screen the app draws itself -- Chromium lays it out correctly there, and the one rule in index.css already covers every element outside a pane.

The open question the design turns on is how the file is chosen: a picker over the project's folder, or whatever file nvim currently has open.

Keyboard-first, so it is a row in actions.ts and a section in help.ts.

Related: the notes mode card is this same screen for a file the app owns. This one is for a file the project owns.

cards.title: Agent state per pane from Claude Code hooks, answered from the manager list
cards.notes: A hook script posts permission_prompt, idle_prompt, agent_needs_input and agent_completed to the app. Main keeps a state per pane, keyed by an environment variable the app sets at spawn. The manager row shows the state and the question text; a key on the row sends the answer to that pane. Bell detection stays as the fallback for shells that are not Claude Code.

cards.title: Pull request status on the Ship card, found from the branch through gh
cards.notes: For each card with a branch and no pull request number, gh pr list --head <branch> finds the number and stores it on the card. For each card with a number, poll gh pr view (state, mergeable, checks, review decision) about once a minute and show one glyph on the card: checks running, checks failed, approved, mergeable, merged. A merged pull request is recorded on the card and never polled again. Open: whether a merged pull request moves the card to Done by itself or only marks it.

cards.title: Discard a card's worktree in one key
cards.notes: On a card in Ship or Doing, one key removes its worktree, deletes the branch, and moves the card back to Todo, after a confirmation like delete. Refuses when the worktree has uncommitted changes, saying so; force needs a second confirmation. Open: whether a pane still running in that worktree blocks the discard or is killed first.

cards.title: Search a pane's scrollback
cards.notes: Cmd+F on macOS opens a small search box at the top of the focused pane; Enter and Shift+Enter jump between matches, Escape closes. Uses the xterm.js search addon. The box gets dir=auto, the key is a row in the actions table, and the help dialog gets the row. Cmd rather than Ctrl because Ctrl+F is the shell's forward-char.

cards.title: Review a card's worktree diff in tig
cards.notes: On a card that has a worktree, one key spawns tig <base>..<branch> in the lowest free pane with the worktree as its working directory, reusing the ship's pane picking. tig comes from Homebrew, so the spawn goes through the login shell like nvim. If no pane is free the key refuses and says so, the same way ship does.

cards.notes: Click a path, or press Alt+O for hint mode (letter labels over every path on screen). Resolve against the pane's live cwd, falling back to the project root. Only existing regular files open. Open with nvim --remote +line in the current window, then switch to nvim mode.

cards.title: Resume each pane's Claude session after a restart
cards.notes:
Restarting the app kills every pane, and every Claude conversation in them has to be found again by hand. claude --continue only finds the latest session in a folder, so two Claude panes on one checkout both come back as the same one.

The token sweep already places each live session on its pane through ~/.claude/sessions/<pid>.json. Keep that map with the session's cwd, save it per pane in session.json (after any sweep that changed it, and once more on Quit), and on launch start each such pane's shell in that folder with claude --resume <id> typed into it. A folder that is gone gets a plain shell and no resume.

Spec: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-22-resume-claude-sessions-design.md

comments.body: PR #76 open. Each pane running Claude at Quit comes back in that conversation: a shell in the session's folder with claude --resume typed, or, in a card's worktree, the card's agent resumed the way a ship starts it. session.json keeps a claude slot per pane, main is its only writer, a 30s grace from the resume covers Claudes that have not written their session file yet, and a failed ps saves nothing. Needs the check by hand in a rebuilt app.

cards.title: A failed board read is a failure, not an empty board
cards.notes:
readBoard turns every reason readFileSync can throw into a board with no cards. A missing file is right -- that is "no board yet". An EMFILE with five ptys and an editor open per project, an EIO off a network folder, a permission that changed underneath, are not: the board draws empty with nothing in the status bar, and the next card you type is written whole over the forty that are still on disk.

Only ENOENT is an empty board. Everything else throws, the way readNotes already does. board-view's readAgain has the catch that reports it -- "Board not opened: ..." with render() still running on the board in memory, so the cards stay on screen.

GitHub issue #45.

Shipped in PR #46. readBoard rethrows anything that is not ENOENT. board:read reaches readAgain's catch, which leaves the cards on screen; commitShipMove reaches runShip's, which says "ship failed: ...". The `board` command had nowhere to put it, so its body now runs inside one try that writes a line to stderr and exits 1 -- that covers writeBoard too, which was stack-tracing for the same reasons.

Out of scope and noted on the PR: readWorktrees has the same defect and main.ts writes its result straight back, so a failed read truncates worktrees.json on launch with no card needed.

cards.title: A command line for the board, so agents can work it
cards.notes:
Shipped in PR #33. `DASHBOARD_BOARD` is on every pane the app opens: the path to a command that lists cards and moves them from a shell — list, add, move, set — over the board of the project you are in. Every decision it makes is a call into board.ts, so a card it writes is a card the app wrote.

The second half is that the app notices. Main watches each open project's .dashboard folder and sends board:change, and the board on screen re-reads without moving your selection. The folder, not the file, because a save renames a temporary file over board.json; and against the bytes the app itself last wrote, or every keystroke on a board would redraw it under your cursor.

Four rules stopped being written twice on the way: columnNamed, isTitle, branchFrom and openBoard. The seeded .dashboard/CLAUDE.md prints the command's own usage rather than retyping it.

Not verified: npm run package. The asar-unpack path is reasoned from the config, not seen — worth one packaged run before merging.

cards.title: Zoom the focused pane to fill the page, and back, like tmux
cards.notes:
Option+F makes the focused pane take the whole terminals grid; pressing it again puts it back in place. Same as tmux prefix+z. The key is a row in the actions table and the help dialog gets the row.

Shipped in #31, branch zoom-the-focused-pane. Alt+F marks the terminals view and the CSS gives the whole grid to whichever pane holds the keyboard, so the zoom follows the keyboard and no pane takes your keystrokes from underneath another one. The four below keep their cells and so keep their size — zooming resizes one shell, not five. The refit sits on the pane's own focus handler, the one place every way in lands: a click on a pane never goes through focusTerminal, and neither does coming back from the board. Not remembered across a restart.

Known cost: renderer.ts is at 596 code lines against the 600 ceiling. The next feature touching it needs the file split first.

cards.title: What each pane last printed, and how long ago
cards.notes:
Main sees every byte of every pty. Keep the last non-blank line and the time it arrived, and thirty shells across five projects fit on one screen: `api . terminal 1, 2s ago, 214 tests passed`. The age is the half that earns it -- `quiet 41 minutes` is how you spot the pane you forgot.

The last line is a guess, and the page should not pretend otherwise. Spinners and progress bars redraw one line forever, so the text can be stale in a way the age will not show. Strip the escape codes, take the last line with printable characters in it, and accept it is approximate.

Shipped in pull request 29, branch pane-last-printed. Every pane is a row on the manager, not only the ones asking: a quiet pane gets the one line it last printed and how long ago, a pane that wants something keeps its block of five. The age is stamped where the pty bytes arrive, so a spinner keeps its pane young. Panes are read only for the rows drawn, and a 30s tick keeps the ages from freezing. Answering a pane no longer takes its row off the list, so the empty selection built for that is gone. Open: projects still start collapsed rather than showing every pane at once.

cards.title: Run a task across projects and collect the results
cards.notes:
Shipped. The manager page has a strip of three named sections along the top — general, board, command — walked by Alt+H and Alt+L from any of them. Behind the third: type one shell command, mark which open projects it runs in with Space, press Enter, and read one row per project saying how it exited and what it last printed. Enter on a finished row opens its last five lines; Escape stops a run.

Main spawns one process per project through the user's shell with -lic, the same PATH reasoning the editor and agent panes already use. It is not a pty and borrows no pane, so a command asked of five projects never touches what is in your shells.

An action's scope gained one non-mode value, manager-page, meaning any section of the manager. The strip keys have to be heard on all three sections and `board` is a mode every project also has, so `hears` now takes whether the page is the manager. `scopesOverlap` is exported for the settings screen's clash warning, so the key matcher and the warning cannot drift. The help dialog takes the same flag, or it would list the strip keys on a project's own board where they are never heard.

Known cost: renderer.ts is at 570 code lines against the 600 ceiling. The next feature touching it needs the file split first — its own card.

Not doing, deliberately: named tasks saved in settings.json (you type the command, it lasts the session), results surviving a restart, and any history of runs.

cards.title: Start a card in its own worktree, in one of the project's panes
cards.notes:
A key on a card in Doing makes a git worktree and a branch for it, and puts one of the project's five panes into that worktree. You work the card there while the other panes stay on the main checkout. No stashing, and two cards can be in flight at once without standing on each other.

Not a project tab of its own: that would mean a second entry in the session, a second row in the tab strip and a second install of everything, for a checkout that lives a few days.

The pane has to say which branch it is on. Five panes that all read `terminal 3` with two of them in worktrees is how a command lands in the wrong checkout. That is the naming card, and this needs it.

Decide how a pane is pointed at the worktree. Sending it `cd` keeps whatever was in the pane and leaves its shell where the project started; restarting it there is cleaner and throws away the scrollback. Also decide which pane -- picked by you, or a free one, and nothing yet knows which panes are free.

The lifecycle is the work, not the git command. When is the worktree removed, what happens with uncommitted changes in it, what happens when the branch merges, and what stops fifteen stale checkouts collecting on disk. The nvim pane stays on the main checkout unless something says otherwise.

Design agreed 2026-09-10. Ship is a new column between Todo and Doing; moving a card there creates the worktree off a freshly fetched base branch, takes a pane you have never typed in, and starts `claude "/work-card <id>"` in it. In-flight state lives on the branch, never on main; a local worktrees.json in userData carries the badge, the pane label and the cleanup list. Spec: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-10-ship-a-card-into-a-worktree-design.md

Shipped in #27. Ship is a new column second from the left: moving a card there makes a worktree beside the project off a freshly fetched base branch, commits the card's move on that branch, and starts an agent in a pane you have never typed into. A local worktrees.json carries the card's badge, the pane's branch label and the Ctrl+Shift+W list, which is the only place a worktree is ever removed. The agent's own instructions live in dotfiles as /work-card and land separately.

cards.title: Manager tab: a board of every open project, editable in place
cards.notes:
Shipped. Ctrl+B on the manager stacks one board per open project under project headings, and the cards are edited where they sit. Cmd+Up and Cmd+Down on macOS, Ctrl elsewhere, say which project the keys are aimed at — macOS takes Ctrl with an arrow for Mission Control before the app is told, Escape goes back to the pane list.

Not a second board: createBoardView once per project, so every editing key already worked, each project keeps its own undo and writes its own file, and the renderer gained no branch — the view hands back a BoardView, so it sits in the same field and shows in the same mode. The manager page has two views now instead of one. Both screens re-read on arrival and loadBoard clears undo on every read, so neither can undo over the other.

isProjectPage stopped reading the mode. It answered "is this the manager?" with mode !== "manager", and a manager that can sit in board mode counted as a project — saved to the session file, listed in its own waiting list, draggable along the tab strip. It reads the slot, which is the thing about the manager that never moves.

Two rules that were written twice are written once now. heldIndex in clamp-index.ts is how a selection survives the list under it being rebuilt, asked by the manager’s rows and by the boards on its board. SELECTED_CARD is exported from board-view.ts, so the name of the card the keys are on cannot be renamed there and left behind here — nothing would have failed, the selection would just have stopped being scrolled to.

Seeding .dashboard walks its files unconditionally and checks each one on its own, so a folder cloned without its docs gets them back. It runs in front of every read, and this page reads every open project at once, on the process that also pumps the panes.

Known cost: on a project’s own board Ctrl+H lists the three new keys and pressing them there does nothing. Their descriptions say "on the manager". A mode of its own is the only way out, and costs more in MODES, MODE_NAMES, BLURBS, modeLabel and focusMode for the same screen.

No filtering and no file watching — every column and every card, and a card an agent writes while you are looking turns up when you come back. PR #23.

cards.title: A saved settings.json freezes every shipped default
cards.notes:
Shipped in PR #26. writeSettings wrote the whole Settings object, so the first time you nudged a font size, every shipped key and every shipped colour went into ~/.config/dashboard/settings.json as if you had picked it — and parseSettings read them back as your choices forever after.

What it cost: PR #23 moves the manager board's project keys to Cmd+Up / Cmd+Down on macOS, because the system takes Ctrl with an arrow for Mission Control. Anyone who had ever set a font size kept Ctrl+Up. The only way out was deleting the settings file, which took the font and the colours with it.

chosenSettings now leaves out anything equal to what this build ships — keys, theme, font and shellCommand, not just the keys the bug was found through — which is what parseSettings has always assumed a missing line means. An explicit null key stays: it means no key at all.

It also gives `written` its meaning back. A file naming every action made every line written, so the written-first sort in withoutDuplicates settled nothing and ACTIONS row order decided who lost a clashing key.

cards.title: Show a waiting pane's tail, and answer it with a keystroke
cards.notes:
Shipped. A waiting row on the manager carries the last five lines that pane has on screen, and a character typed on that row goes straight to its pty — three agents asking at once are cleared without switching tabs. Five lines, not one: an agent asks with a numbered menu whose options move around. The bell comes off as the key goes out, so the row leaving the list is the sign it landed.

Enter still takes you to the pane; keys with names never reach the pty, since the window's lookup claims them first and a word typed at a pane that has stopped asking is a command the shell runs. A dead pane takes no keys — it wants Enter in the pane. tailLines and takesAnswer are the rules, in manager.ts with tests; isBareCharacter went beside isModified in shortcuts.ts, because whether a keystroke is a typed character is a keyboard question; reading the xterm buffer stayed in renderer.ts as wiring, off the live screen rather than the scrollback. help.ts has the blurb and an `Any single key` row, and the keys no binding names are one table now, shared with nvim's.

Known edge: a capital needs Shift, and Shift is a modifier, so `Y` cannot be sent. Digits and lowercase can. PR #22.

cards.title: readBoard swallows every read failure into an empty board
cards.notes:
readNotes now rethrows anything that is not ENOENT, and readBoard one file over still does not: every failure comes back as { board: emptyBoard(), brokenFile: null }. A missing file is "no board yet" and that is right; EMFILE with five ptys and an editor open per project, an EIO off a network folder, or a permission that changed underneath is not.

What it looks like: you open a project whose board holds forty cards. The read fails. The board draws empty with no message, because brokenFile is null and readAgain cannot tell that from a project nobody has made a card in. You assume you are on the wrong project, press n, and type a card title. apply sees the board move and calls save(), and writeBoard replaces board.json with one card. The forty are gone and nothing on screen said a word.

The shape is readNotes's — if ((error as NodeJS.ErrnoException).code !== 'ENOENT') throw error; — and readAgain already has the catch that reports it, with render() still running on the board in memory, so a failed read leaves the cards you had on screen rather than an empty column.

Its own card rather than part of the notes pull request because the fix changes a contract every caller on the startup path relies on: renderer.ts and session.ts have to be read along with it. Raised on https://github.com/naeemba/dashboard/pull/43#discussion_r4024308832.

cards.title: Persian typing in a pane was checked and is fine
cards.notes:
Nothing to fix, written down so nobody investigates it twice. macOS's Persian-ISIRI 2901 layout puts ZWNJ -- the نیم‌فاصله, the one character Persian typing cannot do without -- on Shift+Space, and also on Shift+B. Neither is bound to anything in this app, so both reach the pane.

What does sit on Option is ى, ٱ, two diacritics, and the Persian digits ۰-۹ on the numeric keypad. Those are the ones macOptionIsMeta turns into Esc+key, so they cannot be typed into a pane. None of them is standard Persian orthography and a laptop has no keypad, so macOptionIsMeta stays as it is -- turning it off would cost <A-l> in nvim, which is the reason it was set.

Asked of macOS itself through UCKeyTranslate over every keycode and modifier combination, on 2026-09-09, rather than guessed at.

cards.title: Right-to-left text: fixed everywhere the app draws it, never in a pane
cards.notes:
Reproduced, and it splits in two. The app's own text is fixed. A pane cannot be.

What was wrong where we draw it: nothing in the app ever asked for bidi, so a Persian note ending in a full stop drew the stop at the far left of the line and the sentence read as though it began with a period. One rule now asks -- `body *:not(.pane, .pane *) { unicode-bidi: plaintext }` in index.css. Every element rather than a list of the ones holding typed text, because unicode-bidi does not inherit; the list version was written first and already missed the title bar, the column headings, the settings row, the card detail's column names, the branch line and the Directory-not-found path, and would have missed the notes page next. Order only, so the columns still line up; the four boxes you type into carry dir="auto", which turns the box round as well. The manager's arrow became a span of its own -- sharing the name's span it crossed to the far side of a Persian name and stopped lining up with the row above.

What cannot be fixed: anything inside a pane. xterm.js lays out a grid of cells and reorders nothing, and nvim does not do bidi either -- `:help rileft` says so outright. Writing the algorithm into the grid ourselves is the trap: once screen column 5 is no longer buffer cell 5, the cursor, the selection and the mouse all lie, and you click a word and land four characters away. Not worth reopening. `:set rightleft` only helps a file with no English in it, and the webgl renderer's character joiner would leave the cursor wrong regardless.

So Persian prose belongs on a screen the app draws, not in a pane. That is an argument for the notes mode card, and a card worth writing for reading a project's file in a bidi view. PR #21.

Three ways of fixing it inside a pane were tried and none of them works. Written down so the next person does not spend the afternoon again.

1. A bidi filter in front of the pane -- fribidi, which is the Unicode algorithm as a command line tool and is one brew install away. It reorders the text before the terminal sees it. It fights whatever reordering is already going on, and the two together are a different kind of wrong rather than a fix. Also useless for nvim by construction: nvim addresses the cursor per cell, so a filter in the pipe has no line to reorder.
2. xterm.js's character joiner on the webgl renderer, which is the one API that hands several cells to the text shaper as a single run. Loaded the addon, registered a joiner over every right-to-left run, and the output was identical to the default renderer's. It merges draw calls; it does not change the base direction, and the base direction is what puts the words in the wrong order.
3. An option somewhere in xterm.js. There is none: grep the v6 typings for bidi, rtl and direction and there are no hits.

So the only version that could work is bidi in our own renderer -- reorder each row for display and keep a map between visual and logical columns so the cursor, the selection and the mouse stay honest. That map is the whole job. Without it you put the cursor at the start of a Persian word in nvim, press x, and the character that disappears is from the other end of the word. And nvim would still be half wrong, because nvim does its own layout in logical columns -- where the line wraps, where a table column starts -- so reordering the display leaves nvim's idea of the line and what you see disagreeing.

If it is ever wanted, the narrow version is the one to attempt: display-order reordering only, read-only, behind a setting that is off by default. Good enough for cat, bat, less and an agent's output; explicitly not for nvim. Days of work, and it may come out worse than the honest breakage we have. Not chosen.

cards.title: The waiting list, and Enter jumps to the pane
cards.notes: Shipped. Every pane asking for you, named under its project on the manager page, with Enter landing you in it. goToPane is one function now, shared with the notification click, so the two ways into a pane from elsewhere cannot land differently. isRinging moved to waiting.ts and both the tab strip and this list ask it — before, the rule was written twice and dropping `notified` from one would have stopped the tab going yellow while the manager still listed the pane. cards.title: Say which panes have died
cards.notes: Shipped. A pane that exits now shows up on the manager page as `terminal 1 · exited`, red, and Enter on that row takes you to it to press Enter again. The exited flag has always existed and nothing ever read it; onExit redraws now, which is the whole of what was missing. Dead beats asking: a shell that rings on its way out is listed as exited, not waiting, because answering it finds nothing to answer. The tab does not go yellow for a dead pane — yellow means asking today, and giving it a second meaning is a change to the terminals screen, not this page. PR #18.

cards.title: One row per project, and the lists live inside it
cards.notes: Shipped. One row per open project carrying what its panes want — `dashboard · 2 waiting · 1 exited`, or `quiet`. Enter opens a project to name those panes, Enter on a pane lands you there: right tab, right view, keyboard in the pane, and the bell clears on arrival as it always did. Up and Down walk the flat list. The rules are in manager.ts beside a test — managerRows, alertSummary, managerLines, canOpen, selectedLine — and the DOM is in manager-view.ts, the split board.ts and board-view.ts already have. canOpen is the one place deciding a quiet project cannot expand, so the arrow, the drawn lines and the key cannot disagree. The selection is held as what it is on rather than where it is, so a pane that starts asking pushes the highlight along instead of sliding it onto a different pane. Three ordinary rows in the action table under a new manager scope, so they rebind and the help dialog and settings screen print them untold. No age on the row yet — that needs a per-second redraw and belongs with the last-line card. PR #18.

cards.title: A first tab that is not a project
cards.notes: Shipped. The manager sits at the front of the tab strip where a project sits, with no folder, no five shells, no editor and no board. Ctrl+1 lands on it, Ctrl+O comes back to it, a launch with nothing saved opens on it, and nothing can be dragged in front of it. `manager` is a fourth Mode no key selects, and that one fact carries the change: setMode refuses a view the page does not have, which replaces the dead-project check it used to make, and isProjectPage reads the mode so the session file, the picker, the tab drag and the launch landing all ask one question instead of four. Page.views is a Partial record — three views, one, or none. Not written to session.json, and the empty path is a second lock since parseSession already drops a page with no path. The empty window is gone: that state is the manager, and the sentence saying how to open a project moved to its status bar, reading the key and the wording off the action table. Ctrl+H has its own section for it. Nothing is on the page yet — the lists are their own cards. PR #17.

cards.title: Cards remember when they were made and when they last changed
cards.notes: Shipped. A card carries `createdAt` and `updatedAt`, both ISO, both absent rather than null when nobody knows — a board written before the fields existed reads as unknown and stays that way, and nothing is written for a field a card does not have. `updatedAt` moves in editCard, the one funnel every field change goes through, so renaming one card does not stamp the other thirty. A move to another column ages the card; reordering a column does not. Format documented in .dashboard/CLAUDE.md and the copy in board-store.ts, pinned together by the existing test. PR #16.

cards.title: A card knows its branch and its pull request
cards.notes: Shipped. `branch` and `pullRequest` on a card, typed in with `b` and `r`, shown under the card's title so a Doing column says which of its cards is in flight. The number is a whole number above zero written with or without the `#`; isPullRequestNumber decides that for the file parser and for pullRequestFrom, which the commit and the message explaining the refusal both call. flightParts is the one place that says how the pair reads. Nothing fetches them. PR #16.

cards.title: Fix "Open a new project..." doing nothing in the Ctrl+S picker
cards.notes: Hit Ctrl+S, click "Open a new project...", and the folder dialog opens. Confirmed by hand on 2026-09-07 in a build carrying PR #14. There was never a second cause: the quit question was asked with showMessageBoxSync, which stopped the whole main process, so a folder panel already open could never finish. PR #14 asks it with the async showMessageBox and the panel comes back. No code of its own.

cards.title: Stop the open-folder sheet deadlocking against the Quit confirm
cards.notes: The quit question was asked with showMessageBoxSync, which stops the whole main process until it is answered. A folder panel already open could never finish, so projects:open never replied and the renderer showed "reply was never sent". Measured: the main process sat dead for 4.3 seconds in a stripped-down copy of the window. It now asks with the async showMessageBox: the close is always stopped, and answering Quit calls destroy(), which raises no close to answer again. A second close request while the question is up is ignored instead of stacking another question. PR #14.

cards.title: Notify when something in a pane is waiting on us
cards.notes: Out of the app: a system notification when something needs attention, like a Claude session waiting on an answer. In the app: a small in-app notification, and highlight the tab that is waiting. Shipped: the packaged app is re-signed ad hoc so macOS registers it with Notification Center under the same name as its Info.plist, the banner is raised from main instead of the renderer, and a waiting project gets a pulsing red dot on its tab that stops pulsing under reduced motion. PR #13.

cards.title: A settings screen, with the keyboard shortcuts in it
cards.notes: Every key, the theme, the font and the shell live in ~/.config/dashboard/settings.json, and Ctrl+, edits them from the keyboard. One table in actions.ts names every action once; the handler, the help dialog and the settings screen all read it, so a shortcut is no longer written out in three places. A binding is a string like Ctrl+Shift+K and matches the physical key, so Option+H is Option+H whatever character the keyboard reported. Delete the file and everything is back to how it shipped.

cards.title: Give board cards subtasks
cards.notes: Any card can name another as its parent. A subtask is an ordinary card with its own column, priority and subtasks. Tab attaches, Shift+Tab detaches, o opens a card to see and add its children, and a parent shows a bar of where its subtasks have got to.

cards.notes: Ctrl+H pops up a dialog listing the shortcuts for the screen you are on: the terminal grid, nvim and the board each have their own set. PR #9.

cards.notes: Ctrl+N only ever showed [exited 1]. The pane spawned nvim by name, and an app launched from the Dock has no Homebrew on PATH. nvim now runs through a login shell. PR #8.

cards.notes: urgent, high, medium or low. p cycles it, a colour down the card's left edge shows it, the status bar names it, and s sorts the column urgent first. Sorting is stable, so Shift+up and Shift+down still hold within a priority.

cards.title: Give board cards a description
cards.notes: e opens the card's notes in a textarea. Enter is a newline, Escape commits. The description shows on the card, dimmed, under the title.

cards.title: Clicking a notification takes you to the pane that rang
cards.notes:
The banner says `api . terminal 3 is waiting`, you click it, and the app comes forward on that project with that pane focused. Today the click brings the app up and then you go and find the pane yourself, which is the part the banner was supposed to save you.

cards.title: One clamp, not three: board.ts, board-detail.ts and manager.ts each hold a copy
cards.notes: Shipped. src/clamp-index.ts holds one clampIndex(value, lastIndex) beside one test, and every list in the app reads it: board.ts, board-detail.ts (both the redraw and the arrow keys), manager.ts, manager-view.ts, picker.ts and board-state.ts. The three copies the issue named plus three more found on the way - picker.ts and board-state.ts were the same shape as the others and now read the same, and the card detail dialog wrote the two halves by hand a hundred lines below the copy it shared. cards.title: Send one command to many panes
cards.notes:
Shipped in PR #30. Mark projects on the command screen, type a command once, and Cmd+Enter types it into one free pane of each of them — `git pull` in five repos for one keystroke. Enter is unchanged: a process per project, with the exit codes collected in the rows.

Projects, not panes. The screen already marks projects, so both ways ask the same question and neither can run somewhere the other would have left out.

A free pane is one that has not exited and shows no sign of an agent on it. paneUse reads the two signs it can: looksBusy for an agent still working, and the bell for one that has stopped to ask you something — that second one prints no spinner and no `esc to interrupt`, and is usually pane 1, so without it the command would be submitted as the answer to the agent's question.

What it deliberately does not answer: whether a pane is at a shell prompt. Two kinds of pane count as free and take the line. One running a dev server, a tail, psql or vim. And one whose agent asked you something you have already looked at — going to a pane clears its bell, so the mark is off and the question prints neither busy pattern. Both need the same thing to close: shell integration this app does not have. A longer-lived flag only moves the question to when it clears, and there is no answer to that either. Which is what this card said to decide before building — decided: ship without it, and say so in the help blurb rather than let the words promise more than the code does.

A project that got nothing is named rather than counted, and the two reasons are kept apart: `no free pane in api, web` sends you to look at panes, `api is gone` sends you to reopen a folder.

renderer.ts was at the 600-line ceiling, so this split first: src/pane.ts now holds what a pane is and what can be read off it — the Pane type, the screen readers, and paneUse — with a test. renderer.ts is 587 code lines.

cards.title: Remove a project from the open projects
cards.notes:
Shipped in PR #32. Cmd+W on the manager's list, Ctrl+W elsewhere, closes the project the highlight is on — from a pane row too, since those panes are that project's. The page leaves the tab strip, the five shells and the editor are killed, and the session file is written without it.

It refuses while a pane has an agent working or a question waiting, and names the panes in the way. close-project.ts decides that and words it, and asks paneIsFree — the same predicate the command screen picks a pane by, so a pane that screen will not type into is one this will not kill without asking. What it cannot see is a dev server, a tail or vim, which read as idle here exactly as they do on the command screen; the help blurb says so rather than letting the key promise more.

A closed slot is emptied rather than spliced out and is never given to another project: every pane is named by its slot. The worktree records naming a pane in it give that pane up, the way the launch clears every pane on read, or the card stays in flight with nothing running to finish it. A ship whose git half is still going when the project closes refuses rather than starting an agent in a pane no page has.

renderer.ts was at 597 code lines against the 600 ceiling, so this split first along the seam that file had named: src/page.ts holds the Page type, pane and page building, the map of panes by terminal id and the restyle. renderer.ts is 480 code lines, page.ts is 178.

Not done, deliberately: main cannot refuse the close while a card's ship is mid-git — it is a send with no answer — so that case comes back as a message afterwards instead.

cards.title: Open the focused pane's scrollback in nvim
cards.notes: Ctrl+` writes the focused pane's buffer to a file and opens it in the project's nvim with --remote-tab, over a socket the editor pane now listens on. No keystrokes are sent to the editor: a config that swaps ; and : would have the app press ; and open nothing. nvim's path is resolved once, so the tab opens in about 45ms. Also fixed on the way: a quit nvim left the key hanging for 15s, and the temp file was world-readable. PR #35.

cards.title: Add a manager page as the first tab, giving an overview across projects
cards.notes:
A manager for the dashboard app itself, distinct from the other projects. It sits as the first tab, like every other project, but instead of five shells it shows an overview: what is happening, what is waiting on us, everything.

Done — every one of its nine subtasks shipped. What the page is now, in the order it arrived:

- A first tab that is not a project, holding a list rather than panes. #17
- One row per project, with each project's lists inside it. #18
- The waiting list, with Enter jumping to the pane that is asking. #18
- Dead panes said out loud on the row. #18
- A waiting row carries the pane's last five lines, and a character typed on it goes to that pty. #22
- Ctrl+B on the manager stacks one board per open project, edited where it sits. #23
- Send one command to many panes. #30
- Every pane is a row, quiet ones included, with what it last printed and how long ago. #29
- A strip of three sections along the top — general, board, command — walked by Alt+H and Alt+L. Behind the third: one shell command run across the projects you mark, one row per project saying how it exited. #28

The open question the card was written around — what exactly goes on the page — is answered by the nine above and needs no further review.

The loose end its last subtask named, that projects start collapsed rather than showing every pane, is not true any more: #29 gave every pane a row, and there is no collapse left in manager.ts or manager-view.ts.

Known cost, recorded in CLAUDE.md and not a bug to chase: on a project's own board Ctrl+H lists the three keys that belong only to the manager, and pressing them there does nothing.

cards.title: Panes name themselves
cards.notes:
`api . dev server` instead of `api . terminal 3`. One small change and everything else reads better: the waiting list, the notification banner, the status bar, and which pane is on which worktree.

Shipped in PR #36, branch panes-name-themselves. Two sources rather than the card's three, and paneName is the one place that picks between them: a name you typed on Alt+N wins over the title the program set, because a title is a hint the shell rewrites on every prompt. Blank is not a name either way, which is what makes an empty box the way back to following the title. The number stays in front and the branch stays between it and the name, so a truncated status bar drops what you called a pane before it drops which checkout it is in.

Pane.name is deleted. It was the label worked out once when the pane was built, and the manager read it, so a name that moves could never have reached the list. paneLabel learned that pane six is nvim rather than terminal 6, which is the one place that was ever spelled.

nvim names its own pane after the file it has open, through the same escape sequence, so the status bar says `nvim . board.json` where it said `nvim`. Without that the manager's row and the status bar are one pane under two names.

The dialog is promptOverlay, beside confirmOverlay: the same sheet and the same Enter-or-Escape guard with a box instead of a question. Both of CLAUDE.md's hand-kept lists name it.

Typed names go in the session file. Titles do not -- one dies with the program that set it.

Left out on purpose: the third source, a name from the command that started the pane, because nothing starts commands in panes yet -- that is the startup-commands card. No debounce on the title: a shell writes two per command and the guard drops the repeats, so typing is free, but a program that rewrites its title as it works redraws at whatever rate it prints.

Worth its own card: the manager's rows still show no branch, as before. Now that they carry names it reads worse than it did -- two agents in two worktrees both say `terminal 2 . claude`, and that list is the screen you go to precisely because you cannot see them all at once.

cards.title: Main broadcasts worktree changes so the renderer stops polling worktrees.json
cards.notes:
Shipped in #37, branch worktree-changes-broadcast. setWorktrees in main.ts is the one place the record changes after launch: it assigns, writes worktrees.json and sends worktree:change carrying the records and the folder each pane's shell was started in. The four writers that each did the assign-and-write by hand -- a ship, a removal, a project closing, the dead-worktree sweep -- go through it, and the renderer holds a copy that arrives rather than one it fetches.

The poll on arriving at a board is gone, and onShipped with it: a ship's record write broadcasts on its own, so the callback threaded through page.ts, board-view.ts and cards-view.ts had nothing left to do.

A worktree taken away outside the app is still not an event anything hears, so the sweep for it runs on a five-second timer rather than only when a board is opened. Deliberately a poll: one existsSync per record, against a watcher per worktree whose delete event is not the same on macOS and Linux. fs.watch is the upgrade if five seconds is ever too slow.

worktreesDiffer is the new decision, in worktree-store.ts with tests. Not every writer knows whether it changed anything: closing a project asks every record of that project to give its pane up, and one that never shipped a card hands back what it was given. The hand-written guard that used to sit at that call site is gone with it. The sweep never reaches the predicate -- livingEntries only filters, so a count that has not moved is a list that has not moved.

Not run in the app. Tests, tsc and eslint are clean; the installed build needs a rebuild and restart to pick it up.

Unblocks the discard-a-worktree card and the tig card, which both change worktrees and need the change seen at once.

cards.title: macOS may take Ctrl+1..9 for Mission Control, the keys that jump between tabs
cards.notes:
src/actions.ts, the project-jump rows ship Ctrl+1..Ctrl+9 on the mac side. Mission Control's Switch to Desktop 1..9 are the same keys and come alive once you have a second Space. Where they are alive, Ctrl+2 slides you to another desktop instead of jumping to tab 2 - and project-jump is the most-pressed row in the table.

Same shape as the bug PR #23 fixed for Ctrl+Up and Ctrl+Down, which macOS took for Mission Control and Application windows. That PR wrote the rule down above the table: Ctrl with an arrow belongs to macOS. Ctrl with a digit was not checked.

Checked, and the check did not settle it. `defaults read com.apple.symbolichotkeys` holds Switch to Desktop as ids 118 upwards - but this machine's plist has been edited: ids 118..122 carry modifier 1048576, which is Cmd, not the 262144 that means Ctrl, and only desktops 1 to 5 have an entry at all. Every one reads `enabled = 0`, so nothing takes the keystroke here, and the file cannot say what a stock mac does with Ctrl+1.

So the clash cannot bite on this machine, and on a stock mac it is still an open question. The defaults stay. The rule is written above the ACTIONS table beside the one PR #23 left for the arrows, and the settings screen is the escape if the setting is ever turned on. Ctrl+Shift+1..9 for project-move looks clear either way.

If the defaults ever have to move, it cannot be the swap made for the arrows: Cmd+1..Cmd+9 is already terminal-focus on the mac side, so it needs a different family. actions.test.ts already refuses two actions on one key per screen, so a bad swap fails there rather than shipping.

Shipped in PR #38: the eight-line rule above the ACTIONS table, and the defaults left where they are. No key moved. The card that came out of it - a comment trail on a card, in the app and in the board command - is its own card in Todo.

cards.title: A card keeps a comment trail, written from the app and from the command line
cards.notes:
A card has one `notes` field and nothing else to write in. Everything said about a card over its life goes into that one block of text, so a finding, a decision and the original description are one paragraph after another with nothing saying who wrote which or when. Overwrite it from the command line and what was there is gone.

What this adds is a list on the card: each entry a body and the time it was written. Appended, never rewritten, so an agent recording what it found cannot lose what someone typed by hand. `notes` stays what it is - the card's description, the thing you edit.

It has to be in the `board` command in the same change, because the command is how an agent working a card writes back, and an agent with only `set --notes` will keep clobbering the description. `board comment <id> <text>` to append and `board list` or a `show` to read them back.

Every piece of it is a piece that already exists: board.ts owns the operation and the app's keys call it, board-cli.ts calls the same one, board-store.ts reads and writes the file, and .dashboard/CLAUDE.md documents the field. An old board with no comments on a card reads as none - the same way createdAt is absent rather than guessed.

Open: whether an entry carries an author. Nothing in the app knows who is typing, and an agent could write whatever it liked, so a name would be a field nobody can trust. The time and the text may be the whole of it.

The board is a place where comments are read, so it is also a screen question: the detail dialog is where they fit, and the card front can say how many there are. Ctrl+H gets the key in the same change.

comments.body: Shipped in PR #39. The trail is a list on the card, appended and never rewritten; notes stays the description. c writes one from the board or from inside the open card, o reads them oldest first, and the card front says how many. board comment <id> <text> appends from a shell and board show <id> prints a card with its trail, which is the part board list has no room for. No author on an entry — nothing knows who is typing — and at is absent on a line written by hand, the way createdAt is.

cards.title: Token usage per project: this five-hour window, this week, and all time
cards.notes: Read Claude Code's session logs under ~/.claude/projects (JSONL; each line has usage counts, model, timestamp and cwd). Group by cwd to get per-project totals. Five-hour window is the rolling sum of the last five hours. Week is the sum since the last weekly reset, whose weekday and hour you set once in settings because the logs do not record it. Shown as a manager page section, one row per project with the three numbers, plus the current five-hour figure in the status bar. Tokens only, no dollars: a price table goes stale. Read-only and offline. The log format is Claude Code's own and may shift under an update.

comments.body:
Built, with two changes to the notes above. The figures go on the manager's existing project and pane rows rather than a fourth section, and the week runs Monday to Monday rather than from a reset time set in settings — nothing on the machine records that reset, so asking for it was the only way to know it.

Also per pane: each pane running a Claude Code agent carries what that agent has cost, on its manager row and at the right-hand end of the status bar. Which pane a session is in is not in any log; it comes from the process tree, since claude runs as a child of the shell the app spawned for the pane.

usage.ts is the arithmetic, usage-store.ts the reading, pane-sessions.ts the pane. Measured on this machine: 4362 logs, first sweep 5s, every sweep after it 95ms.

cards.title: Move a card on the board with the mouse
cards.notes: Drag a card between columns and within a column with the mouse, doing what Shift+Arrow does from the keyboard. The drag moves the selection to that card first, so the highlight and the pointer name the same row.

comments.body: Shipped in PR #41. Native HTML5 drag and drop: a card is draggable, a column takes the drop, and dropCard in board.ts lands it on a column and a row. The row rule lives in board-drag.ts with its test — a card is claimed from its middle down, so the bottom half of the last card means the end of the column. A drop into Ship ships, so landsInShip now takes 'drop' beside the four directions. A click moves the selection onto a card and opens its title. Cost: text inside a card can no longer be selected with the mouse, because the card is draggable.

cards.title: A fourth mode: notes, one page of them per project
cards.notes:
A project gets somewhere to write things down that are not a card. Free text, one page, kept with the project rather than on the board: `.dashboard/notes.md` beside board.json, so it commits or is ignored with everything else the dashboard keeps about a project.

It is a mode like the other three, which means it is a row in actions.ts, a fourth entry in the views record, and a fourth Mode in modes.ts -- session.ts checks a restored mode against that same list, so a saved page comes back on the notes screen the way it comes back on the board. Ctrl+T, Ctrl+N and Ctrl+B are taken and Ctrl+N is the obvious letter, so the default binding needs choosing.

Two rules it has to keep. The mode key passes through to the pane once you are already in the mode. And the editor reads event.key for itself, so it needs the isModified guard or a modified key does something in it that it was never meant to.

Ctrl+H is part of the change: a new section with its own blurb saying what the screen is.

It inherits bidi for free: the one rule in index.css covers every element outside a pane, so a page of Persian notes reads correctly the day the mode exists. The editor is a box you type into, so it carries dir="auto" like the other four.

comments.body: Shipped in PR #43. A fourth project view: one textarea filling the page, kept in .dashboard/notes.md beside the board. Ctrl+Shift+N — N names the mode, Ctrl+N is nvim's, and xterm sends no bytes for Ctrl+Shift with a letter so the panes lose nothing. No save key: written 400ms after you stop typing and again when you leave, read back on every arrival so an edit made in a pane shows up. The isModified guard the card asked for is not there because there is no handler to guard — the screen has no key of its own, so nothing reads event.key. MODE_KEYS became PROJECT_MODES, which is what session.ts was really asking it, and writeBoard's temp-then-rename came out as replaceFile so notes.md is replaced whole or not at all. Help, README and CLAUDE.md's two hand-kept lists moved with it.

cards.title: A board whose first read fails is written over by the next keystroke
cards.notes:
readBoard rethrows anything that is not ENOENT now, but the view starts on initialBoardState() -- emptyBoard(), which looks exactly like a project nobody has made a card in -- and readAgain set landedRead = token whether or not the read threw. So busy() said false and every key was live over a board nobody read. First Ctrl+B of the session, EMFILE with five ptys and an editor per project, board draws empty with "Board not opened: ...", press n and one card goes over the forty on disk.

Shipped in PR #48. BoardState gains showsTheFile, the name the notes page already gives the same fact. loadBoard is the only thing that sets it and the only way a read reaches the screen, so the failure path needs no code: a read that threw never assigns state, and neither does one that lost the staleness race. busy() asks the board rather than the view.

It began as a let in board-view.ts and moved onto the state because that file has no test and board-state.test.ts does. With it view-local, the line clearing the flag sat one line below the staleness guard; moving those two past each other hands the keys to a board that never went on screen, with npm test, tsc and eslint all still passing. Four tests now pin it.

Out of scope and noted on the PR: a refused key says nothing -- n bounces silently and "Board not opened: ..." is wiped by the next status write. The notes screen has sayIfStranded for exactly this.

cards.title: A fifth column, Review: a finished card goes there and a pr-loop worktree carries its pull request to merged
cards.notes:
A fifth column called Review, for work an agent has finished but nobody has checked.

When Claude finishes a card, the card moves out of the in-progress column (Doing) into Review. The card's worktree is then closed and removed, and a new worktree is made in its place with a pane assigned to run pr-loop against the pull request that card produced.

If pr-loop finishes successfully, the pull request is approved and then merged. The card moves to Done when the pull request is merged.

cards.title: A which-key overlay: press a key and see what it starts
cards.notes:
Like which-key for nvim. Press a key and the app shows every feature reachable from it, rather than having to open Ctrl+H and read the whole help dialog.

Shipped in PR #50. Hold Ctrl, Cmd or Alt with nothing else and a strip along the bottom names every key that modifier can still start on the screen you are on, each row saying what is left to press. Add a second modifier and the list narrows. It is not a dialog — it never takes the keyboard, so the key you press next still fires. Shift alone does not open it: a capital is typed with Shift. The rows come from the same builder the help dialog uses, so the two lists cannot drift; the 400ms wait is an animation delay rather than a timer.

cards.title: Clean up the numbers on the manager list and fill the empty page
cards.notes: The manager page's rows show raw-looking figures like '40.9M 774M 3.1B' and '466.1M 2.4B 8B' next to 'quiet' — three unlabelled numbers per row, nothing saying what they are, and inconsistent widths so the columns do not line up. Also the rest of the page is empty: the list sits in the middle and everything below it is blank.

cards.title: A pane you typed in should be free again when its shell is
cards.notes: Any keystroke adds a pane to typedPanes in main.ts, and nothing takes it out except closing the project, opening a project into the slot, or removing the worktree the pane sat in. So typing 'clear' or pressing Ctrl+L in the five terminals marks all five as busy for the rest of the session, and the ship refuses with 'every pane in <project> is in use — free one and ship again' while the screen shows five empty prompts. Today the only way out is closing the project and opening it again. The mark is right for a pane where you answered an agent's prompt and your work is still in it — the app just cannot tell that apart from a pane you pressed Enter in once.

comments.body: PR #52 merged 18 Sep. A pane is read against the shell it was spawned with, so a pane you only typed in is free again once its shell is.

cards.title: One answer to whether a pane is busy, not three
cards.notes:
The command screen types on top of a pane that is already running something.

Three things answer "is this pane busy" and they disagree. paneIsBusy in src/ship.ts reads the pty's foreground process, and a ship asks this one. paneUse in src/pane.ts builds busy from isRinging plus looksBusy, which scrapes the pane's screen for an agent's spinner, and freePaneIndex in src/free-pane.ts picks the pane a command lands in from that. workingPanes is the third and is not redundant — only the screen can tell an agent still working from one waiting on you.

What it costs: run npm run dev in terminal 1. Ship a card and the ship skips that pane, correctly. Then open the command screen and send a line to every project. looksBusy finds no spinner, freePaneIndex hands back terminal 1, and the line is typed on top of the running dev server.

The divergence predates PR 52. That PR made the ship's half read the process table, which is the accurate half, and left the other alone — so the fix is to move the command screen's pick onto the same reading rather than to add a fourth answer. The catch is that paneIsBusy lives in main and reads a pty while the command screen picks in the renderer, so whatever carries the answer across the wire is the work.

cards.title: A review that cannot take the worktree yet must try again, not give up
cards.notes:
The sweep read the pull request number out of the worktree's board.json in the half-second before the agent committed it. board.json was therefore uncommitted, git refused to remove the worktree, and the card was marked tried-and-failed for the rest of the run. PR 55 sat in Review with nobody reviewing it until someone asked why.

Two faults behind it.

blockingChanges exempts .dashboard/, which is right for a ship — the Ship move that started the ship is uncommitted in the project checkout — and wrong for removeWorktree, because git counts that folder and refuses. So the app checked, found nothing in the way, and then got a raw `fatal: ... contains modified or untracked files` back from git. The d key on the worktree list fails the same way.

And a swap refused for a dirty worktree is not an answer. The agent commits a second later; the next tick would have worked. Marked for good, it never runs again until the app restarts.

comments.body: Opened as PR #56. changedFiles is git's whole answer to "what changed" and blockingChanges is that minus the .dashboard/ exemption; removeWorktree and worktree:check ask the first one, because git is what refuses them. A swap refused for uncommitted files now un-marks the card so the next tick tries again — every other refusal still keeps the mark. /work-card writes the board and commits it in one command now. PR 55 itself still needs the loop run by hand: the running app marked that card before this fix existed.

Second commit on PR #56: the review agent now moves the card to Done on the branch and pushes it before merging, so the merge carries the column into main. It moved the project's board after the merge instead, and that board is never committed — so main went on saying Review for shipped cards. This repo's own board is in that state for PR #54. The board move and its commit are one command, skipped when nothing is staged and scoped to the board file, the way commitShipMove already does it.

PR #56 merged 19 Sep. changedFiles is the dirty check without the .dashboard exemption, which is the one git's own refusal matches, and a swap refused for uncommitted files un-marks the card so the next tick tries again.

cards.title: A failed readWorktrees truncates worktrees.json on launch
cards.notes:
readWorktrees in src/worktree-store.ts catches every reason the read can fail into [], and main.ts:88-89 reads it and writes the result straight back at launch:

  let worktrees = withoutPanes(livingEntries(readWorktrees(worktreesFile), existsSync));
  writeWorktrees(worktreesFile, worktrees);

So one EMFILE or EIO at launch empties the file, unconditionally, with nobody pressing a key. Three worktrees in flight disappear from the worktree list, and shipping one of those cards again makes a second branch and a second folder -- the orphan the record exists to prevent.

The same shape PR #46 gave readBoard fixes it: only ENOENT is "nothing recorded yet", everything else throws.

readSession and readSettings should stay swallowing: both fall back to a default that is genuinely right when the file cannot be read, and neither writes that fallback back over the file. readWorktrees is the one that does.

cards.title: The ship and the command screen disagree about what a free pane is
cards.notes: Three things answer 'is this pane busy' and they answer differently. paneIsBusy in ship.ts reads the pty's real foreground process, so the ship refuses a pane running 'npm run dev'. looksBusy in waiting.ts scrapes the screen for an agent's spinner or its 'esc to interrupt' line, so the same pane reads free to the command screen's Cmd+Enter and to the close-project refusal — a command gets typed on top of your dev server. workingPanes in working-panes.ts is the third, and that one is not redundant: only the screen can tell an agent still working from an agent waiting on you, which the process table cannot see. So the fix is not one predicate replacing the other two — it is main sending each pane's foreground process to the renderer over the channel that already carries reports the other way, and paneIsFree in free-pane.ts reading both. The divergence predates the typedPanes change; that change made the ship's half accurate and left the other half alone.

comments.body: Stopped: already fixed on main by 625225c (19 Sep, "command screen and close: pick a pane by what is running in it"). The command screen's Cmd+Enter and the close now ask main over panes:read and use the ship's own paneIsBusy, which reads the pane's foreground process. Run npm run dev in terminal 1, send a line to every project: terminal 1 is skipped. Close the project: refused with "terminal 1 npm". looksBusy is now only used for the bell and the working report the review sweep reads. The card's plan of reading the screen too would add nothing: an agent pane already counts as busy, either from its recorded command or from its foreground process. Nothing left to build. Suggest moving the card to Done or deleting it.

cards.title: readBoard turns a failed read into an empty board
cards.notes:
src/board-store.ts line 293 catches every reason readFileSync can throw and returns an empty board. A missing file is 'no board yet' and that is right; EMFILE with five ptys and an editor open per project, an EIO off a network folder, or a permission that changed under you are not, and they come back the same way with brokenFile null, so nothing reaches the status bar.

The cost: you open a project whose board holds forty cards, the read fails, the board draws empty with no message. You assume you are on the wrong project, press n and type a card title. apply sees the board move, save() runs, writeBoard replaces board.json with one card, and the forty are gone.

cards.title: Claude pane on the Agent SDK that renders the chat itself
cards.notes:
A new pane kind beside the terminal pane: it runs a session through @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk (query() in streaming input mode) and the app renders the chat as HTML. Markdown as markdown: tables, highlighted code, images inline, diffs as diffs, tool calls folded to one line that expands. Terminal panes stay xterm.js for shells, nvim and everything that is not Claude.

Why: the terminal pane shows Claude's answers as ANSI bytes; a pipe table stays pipes, an image stays [Image #2]. Swapping the emulator changes nothing; only a structured stream does. A read-only reader fed by the transcript jsonl was the smaller option; rejected because it cannot take input and the TUI's own lines (spinner, usage limit) never reach the file. The VS Code extension and desktop app are closed source, no reuse. OpenCode and the like are different agents, not Claude Code.

First version, bounded: one pane; prompt box with image paste and @file; streamed text, code, tables, images; tool calls folded; permission dialog from canUseTool, keyboard answered, raising the app notification; AskUserQuestion as a form; Esc to interrupt; context bar from getContextUsage(); model and permission mode per pane (setModel, setPermissionMode). No slash commands, no plan mode UI, no /resume picker in this version; resume by session id only.

Fits the other cards: the main session and worker panes (card a639736a) become app code, a query() handle per pane, worker cwd = card worktree, done signal = the result message. CLAUDE.md, rules, skills, hooks, MCP load from cwd via the SDK.

Pin the SDK version. Bump weekly: read the SDK CHANGELOG entries since the pin (github.com/anthropics/claude-agent-sdk-typescript/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md), and skim the Added lines of the CLI CHANGELOG (github.com/anthropics/claude-code/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md) for TUI features worth copying. Measured over 30 CLI versions: about 150 of 2256 entries touch this pane's job, 15 to 20 worth copying; the SDK side is about one Changed entry per release.

Before writing the permission and stream handling, read how getAsterisk/opcode and sugyan/claude-code-webui do it.

Known costs, accepted: the input side is ours (about fifteen small pieces), bugs in it are ours, and each CLI release may add a TUI feature the pane lacks until wired. Scrollback must virtualise: a 169k-token session rendered as DOM stalls the renderer.

cards.title: Main session that dispatches tasks into worker panes
cards.notes:
Each project gets one main session, full height on the left, and a scrollable list of worker panes on the right. The main session is where I talk; it dispatches tasks into fresh panes instead of running them itself.

Layout: main pane left, full height. Right half is a scrollable list of worker panes, as many as dispatched. Keys: Ctrl+1 main, Ctrl+2..9 the first eight workers, j/k past that. A key spawns a new worker pane when there is no task, with a button beside it.

Dispatch: the main session is launched with a name (claude --name main). A session command beside board gives it the glue: session claim returns a pane id; session run <id> "<prompt>" starts claude in that pane with the prompt as the argument, never by typing into a live REPL; session release <id> closes it. Main talks to a worker over SendMessage to its name.

Done signal: the worker's prompt ends with "SendMessage to main when done". A Stop hook in the worker sends the same message regardless, so a worker that forgets or dies on an error still reports.

Permissions: auto mode everywhere. The worker's Notification hook (permission_prompt) calls session notify <id> blocked; the app marks the pane and raises a notification so I can answer it. The app never scrapes pane text for prompts.

Worktrees: a card task reuses the worktree the board already made for the card. A non-card task gets a throwaway worktree, removed after the worker has committed, pushed and opened the PR, never before. Research needs no worktree; it reads the main checkout.

Dispatch rule, one line in main's prompt: a pane is for a task I asked for (do X, review X, research X), never for a lookup main needs mid-task; those stay inline or in the Agent tool.

cards.title: Add a per-project docs directory with one brief spec per change
cards.notes:
Seed per-feature docs for this project and move the existing docs into them.

Layout:

    docs/
      README.md              index: feature, one line, link
      <feature>/
        README.md            files the feature owns, what it does, acceptance scenarios, open questions
        hard-rules.md        only when one exists
        decisions.md         only when one exists
        history.md           one line per merged change: date, PR, why

Only README.md is required per feature; the other three appear with their first entry. Each file stays under 80 lines, history.md exempt; over the cap means the feature is two features.

The feature README owns its file list; docs/README.md is the index only, so a file is claimed in one place.

README.md carries 2 to 5 acceptance scenarios, Given/When/Then, one line each. A change that moves behaviour edits a scenario; the diff shows it.

Every entry in hard-rules.md and decisions.md has a stable id, <feature>-rule-N and <feature>-decision-N, never renumbered. history.md lines, PRs and commits cite the id, so the link survives rewording. Scenarios in README.md stay unnumbered.

For dashboard: about 7 features (panes, nvim, board, notes, remote host, settings, help). docs/decisions.md entries move into each feature's decisions.md; docs/hard-rules.md entries into each feature's hard-rules.md, cross-cutting ones stay in CLAUDE.md. Board card notes and superpowers session specs are the input for history.md lines; the session spec is not the record.

CLAUDE.md gets one line: feature docs live in docs/; a change to a feature's files changes its docs in the same PR.

Outside this card: the rule text goes in dotfiles/claude/rules/ as a global rule, and a hook fails a PR that touches owned files without touching the feature's docs.
