cards.title: Review every decision in the app from first principles
cards.notes:
A first-principles review of the whole app: assume every basic decision is wrong until it earns its place. For each one ask why we do it this way, what it costs the user, and whether there is a better approach. Report only; no code changes. The user picks what to act on.

Stance
- Start from the user's real job: running several projects, each with a main Claude session that dispatches work to worker panes, plus their board, notes and docs. Judge every decision by whether it serves that job, not by whether it is consistent with the rest of the app.
- Recorded decisions (docs/<feature>/decisions.md, hard-rules.md, the CLAUDE.md rules) are the things under review, not the authority. Read each entry's reasoning, then argue against it. Keep it only if the argument fails.
- "It already exists" and "it took work" are not arguments. Neither is "Claude Code does it this way".
- No contrarianism for show: a decision that survives gets one line saying why it survived.

What to review (at least)
- The product itself: is a dashboard of terminals the right shape? Main session plus worker panes, versus fewer, better-supervised agents, versus something else. What does the user still do by hand that the app should do, and what does the app do that nobody uses?
- Platform: Electron, xterm.js, node-pty, the Agent SDK screen alongside CLI panes (two ways to run Claude: is that one too many?).
- Architecture: main/renderer/preload/shared split, IPC design, the socket and CLI, state ownership (what lives in board.json, userData, ~/.dashboard, memory), file watching, the single-window model.
- Work model: the board columns and their rules (Ship, Review, Done-on-branch-first), worktrees per card, the dispatch protocol (claim/run/release, SendMessage reports), pr-loop and merge flow, version bumps on every card.
- UX: keyboard-first rules, modes and mode keys, which-key, the manager tab, the drawer, notes, the Claude screen, settings. Where does the user wait, click twice, or lose their place?
- Process rules: docs per feature with hard-rules/decisions/history, the module-plus-test rule, file-size limit, refusal rules. Do they pay for themselves, or slow every change down?
- Reliability: what breaks on restart, on a crash, on a dead network, with two windows, with a missing folder.
- Security: the socket, panes that run any prompt, permission modes, secrets in env.

Method
- Read docs/README.md and every feature's docs first, then the code where a decision is enforced. Use the app in a demo instance (never the user's running app, workflow-rule-1) for UX claims.
- Ground every claim in a file, a doc entry, a measurement or an external source. Mark what is opinion.

Deliverable

cards.title: Profile the app and report what makes it slow or heavy
cards.notes:
Measure where the app spends CPU, memory and time, find the problems, and report them. No fixes in this card: each finding becomes its own card the user picks from.

Why: the app feels like it could be faster. Replacing Electron was ruled out (2026-11-01): every alternative loses features in use (Chromium's PDF viewer, Chromium's canvas and WebGL speed on Linux, the Node-only Agent SDK). Find out what is slow in the app itself first.

Run it on a demo instance, never the user's running app (workflow-rule-1): a build in out/ or .vite/ with its own user data, on a headless output, the way earlier hand checks were done. Load it the way the user uses it: 4-5 projects open, the manager tab, a main Claude screen with a long conversation, 4+ worker panes streaming output, the board, the drawer open.

What to measure, with numbers before any claim
- Memory per process (main, each renderer, GPU, utility): private memory, not summed RSS, which counts shared pages once per process. What grows over 30 minutes of use, and what never comes back after a project is closed (a leak).
- Renderer CPU while idle and while panes stream: Chrome DevTools Performance traces of the renderer. Long tasks over 50 ms, layout thrash, work done for hidden tabs and hidden panes.
- Terminal rendering: xterm renders through the DOM today (no @xterm/addon-webgl). Frame time and input-to-paint latency while typing and while a pane floods output. Measure it, propose nothing yet.
- Main process: `--inspect` CPU profile. Synchronous fs or child_process calls on the main thread, polling timers, file watchers (count them, check they are closed), IPC message rate and payload size per channel.
- Startup: time from launch to a usable first project, split into main boot, window, first paint, projects restored.
- Tab switch and project open or close: time and what gets rebuilt.
- Claude screen: render cost of a long conversation (markdown re-rendered per message or per stream chunk?), memory held by old messages.
- Bundle: size of the renderer bundle and what is in it.

Also read the code for the usual suspects, each confirmed or ruled out by a measurement: listeners never removed, intervals never cleared, per-keystroke full rebuilds, unbounded arrays or maps (scrollback, logs, session index), JSON.parse and stringify of large files on hot paths.

Deliverable
- docs/performance/README.md: how to reproduce the measurements (commands, flags, load setup), so it can be rerun after fixes.
- A findings report in the PR body and in docs/performance/history.md: each finding has the measured number, where in the code, what the user notices ("typing in a pane lags 80 ms while another pane prints a build log"), and a suggested fix sized small, medium or large. Ranked by user-visible impact.
- One Backlog card per finding worth fixing, with that measurement in its notes. No code changes beyond tooling a measurement needs, e.g. a debug-only timing flag; any such flag is off by default.
- Version bump: patch if tooling was added, none if only docs (the board rule still bumps for a merged card, so patch).
